variants.structure: myth-bust → mechanism → MRI evidence → debate → arthritis payoff → loop + comment question (7 beats)

beats.text: What actually pops when you crack your knuckles?
beats.visual_intent: frame 0: big fist, pop burst, question mark, WHAT POPS?

beats.text: Not your bones. Your joints sit in a capsule of fluid.
beats.visual_intent: joint cross-section: capsule full of fluid

beats.text: Pull the joint apart, the pressure drops, and a gas cavity snaps open.
beats.visual_intent: bones pull apart, bubble snaps open with a burst

beats.text: In 2015, scientists filmed it inside an MRI. The pop happened as the bubble formed.
beats.visual_intent: MRI ring around the joint, bubble appears

beats.text: A 2018 model says a partial collapse could still make the sound. The debate isn't over.
And arthritis? A study of 215 people found no link.
So it's just a bubble. Do you crack yours?
beats.visual_intent: back to the fist; on-screen DO YOU CRACK YOURS?

title_options: What actually pops when you crack your knuckles
Knuckle cracking: a bubble, not your bones
publish.description: An MRI caught the moment a knuckle cracks: a gas cavity forms in the joint fluid. And no, the habit is not linked to arthritis.

cta.decision_reason: the loop line ends on a personal question; commenting is the natural next step and keeps the loop intact

beats.text: What actually pops when you crack your knuckles?
beats.visual_intent: frame 0: big fist, pop burst, question mark, WHAT POPS?

beats.text: Here's the chain. You pull the joint. The fluid inside loses pressure.
A gas cavity forms in a flash. That's the pop. MRI scans caught it happening.
beats.visual_intent: bubble burst inside the MRI ring

beats.text: The bubble stays behind for a while.
And one doctor cracked only his left hand for sixty years. No arthritis in either hand.
beats.visual_intent: two fists, left popping, both healthy
